# **Thermally Adaptive Passive Morphing Rotor Blades for Energy-Efficient Ceiling Fans**

## **Executive Summary**

Autonomous aerodynamic adaptation in residential ceiling fans presents an engineering solution to optimize indoor thermal comfort and energy efficiency without the mechanical complexity, electrical parasitic losses, sensor failure modes, and acoustic penalties associated with motorized pitch mechanisms1. Residential ceiling fans driven by brushless direct current (BLDC) motors operate across a fixed matrix of rotational speeds and static blade geometries, where air delivery is constrained by invariant chord, camber, and pitch distributions1. Developing a blade capable of passive, autonomous shape transformation allows the fan to switch between a low-convection draft mode during cooler ambient temperatures (![][image1]) and an accelerated, high-volume convective cooling mode during warmer conditions (![][image2])1.  
Implementing such shape transformation on a standard 1200 mm ceiling fan operating between 50 and 350 RPM requires resolving a coupled thermomechanical and aeroelastic design challenge. The actuator must generate visible and aerodynamically meaningful geometric deformations—specifically an angular deflection of ![][image3] to ![][image4] in blade pitch or trailing-edge flap articulation—over an indoor ambient temperature swing as narrow as ![][image5], while withstanding centrifugal loads exceeding 100 N per blade, dynamic untwisting moments, and unsteady aerodynamic pressure fields4.

The thermostatic bimetal helical drive is the most robust and production-ready architecture for commercial deployment, offering zero functional hysteresis, high structural repeatability, and complete immunity to functional fatigue across millions of operational cycles5. For high-deflection and rapid-transition prototypes, an antagonistic one-way Nickel-Titanium (NiTi) shape memory alloy (SMA) wire paired with an antagonistic stainless steel return spring provides reliable performance, bypassing the cyclic degradation seen in intrinsic two-way SMA training methods4. Aerodynamic and structural considerations indicate that integrating the morphing mechanism along the outer 30% to 40% of the blade span as an articulated trailing-edge flap isolates centrifugal stresses, limits actuation torque requirements, and produces a 12% to 18% modulation in total air delivery without risking rotor dynamic imbalance4.

## **Candidate Materials and Structures Comparison**

Passive thermal morphing requires solid-state materials that convert ambient heat directly into mechanical work without auxiliary power supplies. In ceiling fan applications, candidate systems must function within a low-temperature band (![][image8]), demonstrate a sharp response over a narrow thermal transition (![][image9] centered around ![][image10]), and withstand millions of aerodynamic load cycles2.

### **Shape Memory Alloys**

Shape memory alloys undergo a diffusionless, thermoelastic martensitic phase transformation between a low-temperature monoclinic martensite phase (![][image11]) and a high-temperature cubic austenite parent phase (![][image12])6. During heating through the transformation window (![][image13]), thermal energy drives an energetic reconfiguration of the crystal lattice, restoring macroscopically deformed shapes against external mechanical loads6.  
Near-equiatomic binary Nickel-Titanium (NiTi or Nitinol, 50.0 to 50.8 at.% Ni) remains the standard for functional performance, yielding up to 8% recoverable transformation strain and work densities exceeding ![][image14]6. The transformation temperatures of NiTi are sensitive to chemical composition: a 0.1 at.% increase in nickel content depresses transformation temperatures by roughly 10 °C7. Commercially available compositions can be tuned so that the austenite start temperature (![][image15]) begins at 26 °C and the austenite finish temperature (![][image16]) concludes at 34 °C, making the alloy responsive to normal room temperatures8.  
Copper-based SMAs, such as CuAlNi and CuZnAl, present lower raw material costs and can also be tailored to ambient temperatures10. However, their polycrystalline microstructure exhibits high elastic anisotropy and coarse grain boundaries that promote localized intergranular stress concentrations10. Under continuous cyclic loading, polycrystalline Cu-based alloys suffer from brittle intergranular cracking and rapid functional fatigue, rarely exceeding ![][image17] to ![][image18] cycles under dynamic stresses10. Iron-based SMAs (FeMnSi and FeNiCoTi) operate via stress-induced ![][image19] phase transformations and offer high elastic moduli, but they require high activation temperatures (![][image20]), display wide thermal hysteresis spans (![][image21]), and offer low recoverable strains (![][image22]). These properties make Fe-based SMAs impractical for room-temperature residential environments.  
The Intrinsic Two-Way Shape Memory Effect (TWSME) allows an alloy to switch between distinct cold and hot geometries without an external bias force6. This behavior is introduced through specialized thermomechanical training regimens, including cyclic isobaric thermal cycling through the transformation temperatures, constrained transformation thermal cycling under fixed parent-phase strains, and controlled plastic over-deformation in the martensitic state6. These training methods generate organized internal residual stress fields and dislocation networks that favor the nucleation of specific martensite variants when the material cools6.  
However, TWSME suffers from structural degradation that limits its suitability for consumer appliances. Because the directional bias relies on internal dislocation tangles, operational cyclic stresses cause these dislocation networks to rearrange and relax over time6. Consequently, spontaneous two-way strain decays by 30% to 60% over ![][image17] to ![][image18] cycles6. Furthermore, the maximum recoverable strain for TWSME is restricted to 1.0% to 1.8%, compared to the 6% to 8% achievable via the conventional One-Way Shape Memory Effect (OWSME)6.  
To address these limitations, an antagonistic bias assembly pairs an un-trained one-way SMA component (wire, torsion rod, or helical spring) with an external structural restoring force, such as a linear steel spring or a compliant cantilever11. This architecture leverages the modulus shift between phases: parent austenite exhibits an elastic shear modulus roughly three times higher than twinned or detwinned martensite (![][image23] versus ![][image24])4.  
When ambient temperatures exceed ![][image16], the stiffening SMA element contracts against the steel bias spring, driving the blade flap or root hinge into its high-pitch orientation4. When temperatures fall below ![][image25], the SMA relaxes into compliant martensite, allowing the steel bias spring to stretch the wire back to its low-temperature position4. This antagonistic configuration bypasses internal dislocation decay, utilizes the full OWSME strain capability, and delivers operational lifespans exceeding ![][image26] cycles without functional degradation6.

### **Shape Memory Polymers and Composites**

Shape memory polymers (SMPs) utilize permanent macromolecular crosslinks (chemical netpoints) alongside switching segments that soften above a thermal glass transition (![][image27]) or crystal melting point (![][image28]). Reversible two-way SMPs can be formulated by incorporating semi-crystalline domains where crystallization-induced elongation and melting-induced contraction operate within internal stress fields.  
However, SMPs possess fundamental physical limitations when deployed in rotating structures. The storage modulus drops from ![][image29] in the glassy state to ![][image30] in the rubbery regime, while recovery stresses rarely exceed 2 to 5 MPa. Additionally, their phase transitions are broad, frequently requiring a temperature change of 15 K to 25 K to transition fully. When subjected to continuous centrifugal acceleration at 350 RPM, rubbery polymers experience rapid viscoelastic creep, cold flow, and stall flutter, leading to dynamic imbalance and structural instability4.

### **Liquid Crystal Elastomers**

Liquid crystal elastomers (LCEs) contain weakly crosslinked polymer networks incorporating rigid, anisotropic mesogenic moieties. Heating past the nematic-to-isotropic clearing point (![][image31]) disrupts nematic alignment, causing reversible, unconstrained axial contractions of 20% to 40% along the director axis without an external bias.  
Despite this large strain capability, LCEs exhibit low elastic moduli (![][image32]), high production costs (![][image33] at chemical synthesis scales) \[unverified claim\], and susceptibility to photochemical and oxidative degradation. Most critically, an elastomer with a 1 MPa elastic modulus cannot support the dynamic pressure fields and centrifugal loads of a ceiling fan blade without undergoing aeroelastic flutter and catastrophic divergence4.

### **Thermostatic Bimetals and Trimetals**

Thermostatic bimetals consist of two metallic sheets with contrasting coefficients of thermal expansion (CTE) bonded via solid-state roll cladding and diffusion annealing5. The active layer is typically an iron-nickel-manganese alloy or high-expansion copper alloy (![][image34]), while the passive layer is an Invar alloy such as Fe-36Ni (![][image35])5. Trimetals add a central copper layer to enhance thermal and electrical conductivity without altering differential strain characteristics5.  
Because thermostatic bimetals rely on differential thermal expansion rather than a structural phase transformation, they do not experience crystallographic slip, mechanical degradation, or measurable hysteresis5. Curvature varies linearly with temperature, providing dependable positioning across decades of service5.

### **CTE-Mismatched Composites and 4D Printing**

Thermally responsive 4D-printed structures utilize multi-material fused filament fabrication (FFF) to deposit adjacent layers of high-CTE and low-CTE polymers, such as thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU, ![][image56]) against polylactic acid (PLA, ![][image57])9.  
While these bilayers demonstrate large shape changes over wide temperature differences (![][image58]), the net CTE differential (![][image59]) produces negligible curvature across a 10 K room-temperature span9. Furthermore, standard PLA softens near its glass transition (![][image60]), experiencing noticeable creep, physical aging, and warpage at ambient temperatures of 35 °C to 40 °C. These tendencies are accelerated by high humidity, making 4D-printed polymers poorly suited for structural rotor components9.

### **Paraffin Wax Actuators**

Paraffin actuators harness the 10% to 15% volumetric expansion of long-chain hydrocarbons undergoing a solid-to-liquid phase transition within a sealed metallic cylinder. By formulating specific alkane blends (such as tetradecane, octadecane, and eicosane), the melting transition can be centered between 28 °C and 32 °C. An internal elastomeric diaphragm translates this volume expansion into high-force linear motion, generating operating pressures exceeding 15 MPa.  
However, paraffin actuators introduce significant mass penalties (50 to 120 g per unit), rely on elastomeric seals vulnerable to dry-rot and extrusion, and exhibit slow thermal response times (60 to 180 seconds) due to the low thermal conductivity of organic waxes (![][image61]). Furthermore, when mounted on a rotor spinning at 350 RPM, centrifugal acceleration can cause centrifugal phase segregation in the partially melted wax, introducing localized mass unbalances that undermine dynamic stability4.

## **Mechanical Loading and Aeroelastic Feasibility Analysis**

Operating a 1200 mm ceiling fan up to 350 RPM exposes the blade structure to continuous centrifugal body forces, steady and unsteady aerodynamic lift and drag, pitching moments, and dynamic untwisting moments4. Candidate morphing mechanisms must maintain dimensional stability against these loads to prevent aerodynamic flutter and rotor unbalance4.

### **Morphing Location Trade-Offs**

Configuring the blade for whole blade continuous twist requires a flexible structural spar enclosed in an elastomeric skin. While this approach optimizes spanwise circulation, the low torsional stiffness leaves the blade susceptible to centrifugal untwisting and dynamic flutter. Furthermore, continuous elastomeric materials degrade when exposed to prolonged indoor ozone and UV radiation.  
Implementing a root pitch hinge places the entire blade on a radial pivot at the hub. This maximizes aerodynamic authority, as adjusting the root pitch angle alters the angle of attack across the entire span4. However, the pivot bearings and actuator must support the full 107.5 N centrifugal load and the 0.082 N·m untwisting moment4. In small thermal actuators, bearing friction under high centrifugal loads can lead to stick-slip behavior that impedes smooth shape adjustment.  
A morphing winglet or tip fence modifies tip vortex shedding and induced drag. While effective for reducing acoustic emissions by 1.5 to 2.5 dBA, this configuration alters room air delivery by less than 3%, making it insufficient as a primary airflow control mechanism.  
Integrating an articulated trailing-edge flap along the outer span (![][image189]) represents the most balanced design14. The rigid forward section (75% of chord) carries all primary centrifugal, bending, and thrust loads4. The morphing flap controls effective camber over the aerodynamically dominant outer portion of the blade, where dynamic pressure is highest4. The flap's small mass (15 g) keeps centrifugal body loads low (9.07 N at 350 RPM), reducing the required actuation force and isolating the primary blade structure from mechanical failure modes4.

### **Aerodynamic Sensitivity to Pitch and Camber**

Low-solidity ceiling fans operate within a baseline pitch envelope of ![][image190] to ![][image191]4. Within the unstalled regime (![][image192]), volumetric air delivery scales almost linearly with effective pitch:  
![][image193]  
A ![][image3] pitch increase on a ![][image194] baseline represents a ![][image195] change in geometric pitch, producing an empirical ![][image196] to ![][image197] increase in volumetric air delivery (![][image198])4.  
Articulating the trailing edge downward by ![][image199] to ![][image200] increases section camber by approximately 2.5% to 3.5%, shifting the section lift coefficient upward by ![][image201] without precipitating boundary layer separation. Because induced and profile drag scale with ![][image202], this camber increase raises rotor torque by 14% to 18%4. For modern BLDC ceiling fans operating under constant-RPM closed-loop control, the drive draws 3.5 to 5.0 W of additional power to sustain speed, remaining comfortably within motor thermal limits2.

### **Thermal Kinematics: Warm vs. Cool Operation**

The morphing direction aligns with domestic comfort requirements across seasonal temperature swings:  
In warm ambient conditions (![][image203]), the actuator deflects the trailing edge downward, increasing effective blade pitch from ![][image190] to ![][image191] and enhancing profile camber4. This increases downward air velocities to 1.2–1.8 m/s at occupant level, enhancing skin convective heat transfer and sweat evaporation to provide a physiological cooling effect of 2.0 K to 3.5 K16.  
In cool ambient conditions (![][image204]), the mechanism returns the blade to a flat profile with reduced pitch (![][image205]). This mode lowers downward velocities below 0.25 m/s, preventing uncomfortable winter drafts while maintaining air circulation to eliminate ceiling thermal stratification1.

Analysis of granted patents and published applications confirms that there are no active claims covering domestic ceiling fan rotor blades that passively adapt their camber, pitch, or trailing-edge geometry via integral shape memory alloys or thermostatic bimetallic elements without external sensors or electronic actuators1. This leaves clear patent white space for self-contained, thermally autonomous morphing ceiling fan blade architectures.

## **Reliability, Durability, and Regulatory Safety Engineering**

Commercializing a morphing ceiling fan requires designing for a 10-year service life under typical operating and environmental conditions in the Indian market2.

### **Fatigue and Degradation Mechanisms**

The mechanism must withstand two distinct fatigue environments over a 10-year period:

> * Thermal Low-Cycle Fatigue: Approximately 3,650 to 7,300 thermal cycles, assuming one to two room heating-cooling cycles per day. This governs phase transformation stability and bimetal creep behavior5.  
> * Mechanical High-Cycle Fatigue: At an operational speed of 350 RPM, the rotor completes ![][image213] revolutions per hour4. Over 10 years at 7 hours of daily runtime, the blades accumulate ![][image214] rotational cycles4. This loading regime dictates the fatigue life of blade roots, hinge pins, and return springs under aerodynamic turbulence and gravity-sag reversals.

In shape memory alloys, repeated thermal cycling through the phase transformation introduces localized micro-plastic slip dislocations around internal grain boundaries6. This functional fatigue can cause transformation temperatures to drift upward by 2 °C to 4 °C, reduce recoverable strain, and lower peak recovery forces6. To ensure stable operation over 5,000 thermal cycles, cyclic tensile strains must be restricted to ![][image215], and cyclic recovery stresses kept below ![][image216]4. Operating within this conservative window preserves transformation repeatability over long lifespans6.  
Thermostatic bimetals do not suffer from functional phase fatigue, as their deflection is governed entirely by linear differential thermal expansion5. However, sustaining high mechanical stresses at peak summer temperatures can induce mechanical creep. Operating stresses must therefore remain below the material's elastic limit (![][image217] versus a yield strength of 500 MPa) to maintain stable calibration across decades of use5.

### **Environmental Durability in Indian Conditions**

Ceiling fans in India encounter challenging operating conditions: ambient summer temperatures up to 45–48 °C, monsoon relative humidity exceeding 95%, coastal salt air, and airborne dust2.  
Galvanic corrosion presents a key reliability concern: thermostatic bimetals and Nitinol have noble electrochemical potentials (+0.05 to \-0.15 V vs. SHE) that differ significantly from typical 6063-T6 aluminum blades (-0.75 V) or mild steel blade brackets (-0.44 V). Direct mechanical contact in humid conditions will accelerate galvanic corrosion on the aluminum mounting points. To prevent this, all SMA or bimetal assemblies should be isolated using non-conductive, glass-filled polyoxymethylene (POM/Delrin) bushings, or protected with high-dielectric epoxy e-coatings across mounting interfaces.  
Nitinol displays excellent corrosion resistance, as titanium forms a passivating titanium dioxide (![][image218]) surface film that protects against humidity, airborne salts, and microbial attack8. For thermostatic bimetals, the high-expansion active layer (FeNiMn alloy) contains iron and manganese, making it susceptible to surface oxidation in humid environments. Specifying an 8–12 ![][image219]m nickel electroplating layer per ASTM B456, or using corrosion-resistant austenitic formulations (such as the Shivalik TB 1555 series), provides adequate moisture protection5.

### **Temperature Overshoot and Fail-Safe Architecture**

Peak indoor temperatures in uncooled spaces can reach 45–48 °C, which exceeds the normal 25–35 °C morphing window. If temperatures exceed ![][image16] (![][image84]), the actuator reaches its design stroke limit. To prevent mechanical damage, the mechanism must include internal travel stops at the maximum design pitch (![][image220]). An integrated compliance cartridge (an inline spring relief) absorbs any additional thermal expansion, protecting the bimetal strip or SMA wire from plastic deformation.  
The antagonistic bias spring also functions as a fail-safe. If an SMA wire fractures or loses anchor tension, the bias spring automatically pulls the flap or blade to a neutral, low-drag aerodynamic pitch (![][image221]). This prevents the fan from getting stuck in an asymmetric or high-pitch configuration that could overload the BLDC motor or create aerodynamic instability4.

### **Dynamic Balance and Rotor Symmetry**

Dynamic rotor unbalance is a critical failure mode for morphing ceiling fans. If one blade morphs to ![][image222] while an adjacent blade only reaches ![][image223], the resulting thrust asymmetry will cause severe dynamic wobble, generate downrod vibration, and accelerate bearing wear2. Blade tip vertical tracking must remain within ![][image224] across all speeds and temperatures2.  
To achieve this level of consistency, bimetal coils and SMA springs must be sorted into matched sets of three during production, with thermal deflection rates matched within ![][image225]3.

### **Regulatory Safety Standards**

Ceiling fan designs must satisfy mandatory safety and performance standards:

> * **IS 374:2019 (Electric Ceiling Type Fans — Specification)**: Mandatory under the Indian Quality Control Order (QCO)3. For a 1200 mm fan, minimum air delivery must meet or exceed ![][image226], and the BEE 5-star service value must be ![][image227]2. The morphing mechanism must not create excess drag that reduces energy performance below this threshold. Additionally, the suspension system must withstand a sustained tensile load of 1000 kg and a torsional torque of 500 kg-cm without damage2.  
> * **IS 302-2-80 / IEC 60335-2-80 (Safety of Household and Similar Electrical Appliances — Fans)**: Specifies mechanical overspeed testing at 1.25 times rated RPM (438 RPM for a 350 RPM motor) for 15 minutes. The morphing blades and retainers must survive this overspeed test without throwing parts, experiencing permanent deformation, or losing dynamic balance.

## **Detailed Mechanical Design Concepts**

Two practical mechanical architectures were developed for prototype evaluation, each utilizing a distinct method to integrate thermal morphing into the blade assembly.

### **Concept A: Helical Bimetal Rotary-Drive Trailing-Edge Flap**

Concept A uses an articulated trailing-edge flap located along the outer span (![][image228]), driven by a calibrated thermostatic bimetal helical coil housed within a streamlined pivot capsule5.  
The forward 75% of the airfoil is a rigid 6063-T6 aluminum extrusion that attaches directly to the hub, carrying all centrifugal and primary bending loads4. The trailing-edge flap (spanning 25% of chord) is molded from lightweight ABS (![][image229]) and supported on stainless steel hinge pins running in POM bushings4.  
The bimetal coil is wound from high-sensitivity strip (![][image95], width ![][image230], thickness ![][image96], flexivity ![][image85])4. Its inner end is fixed to an arbor anchored in the main spar, while its outer end forms an offset drive pin that engages a slot on the flap.  
As ambient temperature rises from 25 °C to 35 °C, differential expansion rotates the coil by ![][image231], deflecting the flap downward to increase section camber and lift4. Air vents in the leading edge direct airflow over the coil to maintain thermal coupling with the room. Because the bimetal strip possesses inherent two-way elastic stiffness, no return spring is needed5.  
This configuration provides high reliability, zero functional fatigue drift, linear response, and consistent tracking over time5. Packaging the 250 mm strip does require an enlarged hinge fairing (![][image232]), which introduces a small aerodynamic drag penalty along the flap hinge line.

### **Concept B: Antagonistic NiTi Wire \+ Bias Spring Root Hinge**

Concept B implements a variable-pitch blade root pivot. The entire blade rotates about an internal pitch spindle via an internal NiTi SMA actuator wire paired with an antagonistic steel extension spring4.  
The blade connects to the hub through a 7075-T6 aluminum spindle supported by dual sealed deep-groove ball bearings and a thrust washer that carries the 107.5 N centrifugal load4. A straight 100 mm NiTi SMA actuator wire (![][image67], ![][image233], ![][image234]) extends spanwise through an internal root chamber8. The inboard end clamps to the hub base, while the outboard end connects to a 25 mm pitch control horn4. A parallel stainless steel extension spring continuously biases the horn toward a low-pitch stop (![][image200])4.  
Below 24 °C, the NiTi wire is in its compliant martensitic state (![][image235])4. The bias spring overcomes the wire and holds the blade against the low-pitch stop. As room temperature rises past 27 °C into the 33 °C range, the wire transforms to parent austenite (![][image182]), contracting axially by ![][image236] with up to 100.5 N of recovery force4. This overcomes the bias spring and rotates the blade by ![][image118] against an adjustable high-pitch stop (![][image237])4. Cooling below ![][image25] allows the bias spring to extend the martensitic wire, returning the blade to low pitch.  
Concept B generates high actuation forces, provides clear two-state positioning, and conceals all components within the hub root profile4. However, it requires precise bearing fits to handle high centrifugal thrust without binding, along with custom-formulated NiTi wire to ensure the transformation occurs reliably within the 27–33 °C window8.

### **Fabrication and Assembly Protocol**

The physical prototype is constructed using standard workshop tools and modified production components:  
To modify the baseline blades, take three standard 1200 mm aluminum fan blades from an Atomberg fan. Using a CNC router or hand rotary tool, machine a slot along the outer trailing edge of each blade (![][image243], span ![][image244], chord depth ![][image245]). 3D print replacement trailing-edge flaps from PETG (15% gyroid infill, 1.2 mm perimeter shells) to keep the mass of each flap under 15 g4.  
To form the bimetal actuator (Concept A), cut the Shivalik TB 2011 strip to a developed length of 250 mm5. Wind the strip around a 10 mm brass rod to produce a 4-turn spiral coil. Heat-treat the coiled strip in a workshop oven at 180 °C for 60 minutes, then allow it to cool slowly to room temperature to relieve residual bending stresses5.  
To prepare the NiTi SMA wire (Concept B), clamp the wire into a rigid steel fixture to set a straight shape. Heat the restrained wire in a muffle furnace at 500 °C for 15 minutes, then quench it immediately in room-temperature water to lock in the austenitic parent state7. Pair the wire directly with the steel bias spring during final assembly, avoiding intrinsic two-way training methods6.  
During mechanical assembly, secure the components using M2.5 stainless steel fasteners. Install POM or PTFE shoulder washers at all contact points between the aluminum blade and the thermal actuator components to prevent galvanic corrosion.

### **Experimental Test and Validation Protocol**

The prototype validation process evaluates mechanical performance across three testing stages:

                          TEST VALIDATION PROTOCOL STAGES  
                            
\+-------------------------------+-------------------------------+-------------------------------+  
| PHASE 1: Static Chamber Test  | PHASE 2: Dynamic Spin Test    | PHASE 3: IS 374 Airflow Test  |  
| \- 15 °C to 45 °C thermal box  | \- 50 to 350 RPM on BLDC stand | \- Anemometers 1.5 m below fan |  
| \- Measure laser deflection    | \- Verify tip tracking \< 2 mm  | \- Airflow at 20 °C vs. 35 °C  |  
| \- Quantify angular hysteresis | \- Confirm dynamic balance     | \- Verify BEE compliance       |  
\+-------------------------------+-------------------------------+-------------------------------+

The first phase conducts static benchtop characterization within a sealed acrylic thermal chamber (![][image246]) heated by a variable temperature air source. The internal temperature is stepped from 15 °C to 45 °C in 2 °C intervals, holding each step for 3 minutes to achieve equilibrium. A laser diode reflects off a mirror mounted on the flap toward an external grid 2.0 meters away, measuring angular deflection and hysteresis over both heating and cooling cycles.  
The second phase mounts the modified three-blade assembly onto the BLDC test hub to evaluate rotational balance in ambient air. The fan is run from 50 RPM to 350 RPM in 50 RPM increments, recording electrical power draw with a digital wattmeter4. An optical tachometer and stroboscopic camera track blade tip vertical positions, verifying that dynamic tip tracking remains within ![][image224] across the full speed range2.  
The third phase evaluates total air delivery in accordance with IS 374:2019 test procedures3. A traverse array of digital vane anemometers is positioned 1.5 meters beneath the fan assembly2. Air velocity measurements are recorded across multiple radial points, first at a cool baseline temperature (![][image247]), and then after heating the room to 35 °C using auxiliary space heaters32. Integrating the velocity profiles across the swept disk area will determine whether the morphing blade achieves the target 12% to 18% increase in total air delivery (![][image248]) while maintaining BEE 5-star efficiency standards2.
